originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site, slug learn-agent-context-engineering, for a reader whose agent starts forgetting, repeating itself, and drifting off course on long tasks. Terminal task: design a context budget for one real long task, and carry that task to completion using external notes plus compaction. Six lessons on context rot, the write/select/compress/isolate levers, when compaction loses what mattered, structured note-taking as memory outside the window, subagents as a CONTEXT-ISOLATION device, and assembling a context budget for a real task. Do not teach harness construction, and do not teach orchestration, parallel fan-out, or result synthesis — a later course orchestrating-agents owns that. Every factual claim must come from a source fetched during the authoring session; teach mechanism and judgment rather than the click-path of any current product.
learnerBrief: The reader already runs agents on real work and can operate one competently — this is not an on-ramp. Their problem appears only past a certain task length: the agent re-reads files it already read, re-argues decisions that were settled, quietly stops honouring a constraint from the start of the session, and finishes somewhere adjacent to the request. Their working theory is usually that the agent 'ran out of room' or needs a firmer instruction, and both readings send them toward repairs that make the window larger. The course has to replace that model with an accurate one (recall degrades continuously as input grows, measured on current models), give them a sorting procedure so 'the window is filling' becomes a specific cheapest-lever choice, and end in a written artifact they have actually run a task against. It must stay out of harness construction and out of multi-agent orchestration, which means subagents appear only as a wall that keeps noise out of the main window.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request named the target reader's symptoms in their own terms (agent forgetting, repeating itself, drifting on long tasks), stated the terminal artifact (a context budget for one real long task, carried to completion with notes plus compaction), fixed the lesson count and the six themes, set the concept ceiling at roughly seven per lesson, declared the reader already runs agents so this is not an on-ramp, and drew two explicit topic boundaries (no harness construction, no orchestration or parallel fan-out). That is a starting point, a goal, and constraints — not a topic name.

learnerModel.targetReader: Someone who already delegates real multi-step work to a coding agent and can read its output, whose runs degrade in a specific way once a task outgrows one comfortable session.
knownConcepts: Running an agent on a multi-step task and reading what it did
Running commands their agent tool provides, such as a slash command or a CLI invocation
The idea that a model has a context window with some size limit
Writing a task description clear enough for an agent to act on
unknownConcepts: How attention is allocated inside a model, or any model internals
Building or modifying an agent harness, loop, or session machinery
Orchestrating several agents in parallel and synthesising their results
Retrieval engineering, embeddings, vector stores, or RAG pipeline construction
Programming beyond reading a file and following a shell command
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: Their own agent tool, their own repository or working directory, and a text file for notes. The course assumes no embedded sandbox, no API access, no specific vendor, and no ability to change the agent's implementation — every technique is available to someone who can only operate the tool, not modify it.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Open a fresh session in a real project and produce a written inventory of what occupies the context window before typing any task, with a size against each item and a note of which items the intended task actually needs.
noviceRamp: Lesson 1 bridges from the reader's own observed symptoms to the mechanism: it opens on the degraded run they already recognise, then supplies the measurements, so context rot arrives as an explanation for something they have seen rather than as a new concept to accept on authority.

Every measurement is stated with its experimental setting attached and an explicit note on whether it bounds the effect or typifies it, so a reader who cannot evaluate the papers still knows not to carry the numbers to their own task.

Product surfaces appear only as illustrations of a mechanism and are stamped with a date, so a reader whose tool differs can still act: each exercise asks them to find their own tool's equivalent from its current documentation rather than to run a named command.

The first independent action needs only reading a breakdown their tool already provides, or estimating from file lengths on disk if it provides none — it requires nothing from the unknown-concepts list.

Subagents are introduced in Lesson 5 purely as a boundary that keeps noise out of one window, with the orchestration reading named and excluded in the opening paragraph, so a reader does not leave believing this course covered multi-agent work.

scope: Covers why filling a context window degrades an agent rather than helping it, the four levers (write, select, compress, isolate) and their relative cost, how to predict what a compaction boundary keeps and place load-bearing state where it cannot be reached, how to write a progress note a memoryless session can resume from, subagents strictly as a context-isolation device with the boundary's costs priced, and how to assemble, run, and revise a context budget for one real task. Deliberately excludes harness construction (the loop, the tool layer, session machinery), orchestration of multiple agents, parallel fan-out and result synthesis, retrieval and RAG pipeline engineering, model internals, and any vendor's UI as a procedure to follow.

evidence: Anthropic, 'Effective context engineering for AI agents' (published 2025-09-29, re-read in full 2026-08-23) — defines context engineering, the attention budget, compaction, structured note-taking, and the 1,000-2,000 token subagent return.

Anthropic API 'Compaction' documentation, retrieved 2026-08-23 — server-side compaction is in beta behind the dated header compact-2026-01-12, supported on the claude-opus-5 / claude-sonnet-5 / claude-fable-5 generation, with a documented minimum trigger of 50,000 input tokens; this is a 2026 feature that did not exist when the engineering post was written.

Anthropic API 'Context editing' documentation, retrieved 2026-08-23 — states that server-side compaction is now the primary strategy and positions tool-result clearing (clear_tool_uses_20250919) and thinking-block clearing (clear_thinking_20251015) as the fine-grained alternatives.

Claude Code 'Explore the context window' documentation, retrieved 2026-08-23 — publishes a per-mechanism 'What survives compaction' table including current per-skill and total re-injection caps, which is the mechanism-level evidence Lesson 3 is built on and which did not exist in the 2025 sources.

'Classifier Context Rot' (arXiv 2605.12366, submitted 2026-05-12) — measures long-context degradation on Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4, and Gemini 3.1, establishing that the effect is a property of the 2026 frontier generation rather than of superseded models.

'Distractor-Aware Truncation' (arXiv 2608.03297, submitted 2026-08-04) — read during sourcing as a current check on whether 'shorter context is better' holds under different truncation protocols; informed the decision not to overstate the trim-everything advice.
topicCurrency.staleRisk: Highest risk: the Claude Code compaction survival table (per-skill 5,000-token and 25,000-token total re-injection caps, and which mechanisms are re-injected versus lost) — these are version-specific and the page is versioned rather than dated. Next: the compaction beta header compact-2026-01-12, the 50,000-token minimum trigger, and the strategy identifiers clear_tool_uses_20250919 / clear_thinking_20251015, all of which are dated strings. Next: the /context, /usage, /compact, /clear and /autocompact command surface and the shape of the /usage session block quoted in Lesson 6. Next: the subagent and fork semantics in Lesson 5, including what a fork inherits. Lower risk but worth re-checking: whether newer model generations shift the measured degradation curves enough to change Lesson 1's framing, and whether the write/select/compress/isolate vocabulary remains the common frame. Lowest risk: the lost-in-the-middle U-shape and the mechanism-level account of what a compaction boundary does to message history.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: Two mermaid diagrams, both load-reducing rather than decorative. Lesson 2 draws the four levers as movements relative to the window boundary, because the write/select pair and the isolate lever are defined by direction of travel and a flat list hides that write and select are inverses while isolate is the only lever creating a second window. Lesson 5 draws the subagent boundary as two narrow arrows, because the entire teaching point is that the boundary is symmetric and readers reliably see only the outbound half; a table would have listed both costs without making the symmetry visible. Lessons 1, 3, 4 and 6 deliberately use tables instead: their content is per-item classification (four failure modes, the per-mechanism survival table, the four note sections, the six budget categories), which is what a table is for, and a diagram would have added shape without adding relationships. Lesson 3 additionally carries the one hotspot interaction, which reuses the diagram idiom for a judgment rather than for exposition.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the course-matrix design doc — six lessons against six fixed themes, with the terminal task specified — and this was a non-interactive run, so it was auto-confirmed. No human reviewed the lesson order, the coverage, or the depth before the prose was written. The DAG and load balance were checked mechanically and the themes are coherent, but if the intended reader needed, say, a lesson on selecting context (retrieval) rather than the budget lesson, nothing in this process would have caught it.

Lesson 6's terminal task cannot be completed in one sitting and has no verification the reader can run against anything but their own honesty. It asks for a multi-hour task crossing a real compaction boundary, and a reader who does the paper exercise without the run gets the vocabulary and none of the calibration. The rubric asks them to state what the budget cost against what it saved 'including the case where it saved little', which is the best available guard, and it is still self-report.

The most durable-feeling content in Lesson 3 — the per-mechanism compaction survival table — is the most version-fragile thing in the course. The 5,000-token per-skill cap and the 25,000-token total are current for one tool as of 2026-08-23 and will move. The lesson mitigates this by stating the underlying rule (disk survives, message history does not) as the thing to remember and flagging the numbers as version-specific, but a reader who takes the table as the lesson will be wrong within a release or two.

Lesson 1's headline numbers come from experiments whose conditions are far more extreme than the reader's situation: 800K tokens of adversarial padding, deliberately irrelevant injected trajectories, up to 30,000 filler tokens. Each is labelled as a bound rather than a forecast, in the prose and again in the glossary entry for 'degradation'. That labelling is the only thing preventing a reader from quoting '13.9%-85%' as what to expect, and prose labels are weaker than not having the numbers at all.

The course teaches subagents as a context boundary only, and a reader who has never used one may finish Lesson 5 able to price the boundary without being able to construct a good delegation. The worked example gives one full delegation message with its four elements annotated, which is one instance; a reader whose tool exposes delegation differently has to bridge that themselves.
followUpChecks: Re-verify the Lesson 3 survival table against the live Claude Code context-window page, since its caps and per-mechanism outcomes are the course's most version-fragile claims; if the table has changed, the rule underneath should still hold and only the illustrative numbers need updating.
Re-check the compaction beta header, the 50,000-token minimum trigger, and the context-editing strategy identifiers, all of which are dated strings likely to have moved.

Have a reader who has actually completed Lesson 6's terminal task report which budget category was furthest from its allocation and which trigger failed, and fold real cases into the worked example if the config-error trigger hole turns out to be unrepresentative.
Watch whether a newer model generation changes the shape of Lesson 1's degradation claim enough to require rewriting the framing rather than just refreshing the citation.
Confirm with the owner of the planned orchestrating-agents course that Lesson 5's boundary holds and that nothing here pre-empts its treatment of delegation.

acceptanceReview.terminalTask: The reader writes a context budget for one of their own long tasks — six named categories, each with an allocation, a lever, and a trigger executable without a judgment call — then runs that task to completion across at least one real compaction boundary, using a four-section note to carry state across it, takes per-category readings at checkpoints, compares the result against the budget, and revises at least one trigger with the revision traced to a specific event in the run. The deliverable is a revised budget plus a completed task, and the rubric requires them to name one specific thing the note carried that the compaction summary did not.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Three interaction blocks across six lessons, each on a misconception that would otherwise survive the reading. The agentmentor-check in Lesson 1 ('Separate length from retrieval failure') exists because the reflex after learning about context rot is a retrieval fix, and the EMNLP result specifically rules retrieval out as the sole cause — each wrong option is a real repair someone would attempt, and the feedback explains why the mechanism does not match. The agentmentor-hotspot in Lesson 3 ('Click what the boundary consumes') puts the survival rule on a diagram because readers judge survival by emphasis and recency rather than by loading mechanism; the three wrong nodes cover the three plausible misreadings (disk-loaded material, accumulated memory, the boundary event itself). The agentmentor-check in Lesson 5 ('Judge which task survives delegation') is there because the token asymmetry tempts readers to delegate by size, and the four options separate size from coupling — including one near-miss (documentation reading) that has the right volume shape and fails on specification. Two agentmentor-action cards: Lesson 2 (reasoning_audit) probes whether the reader actually applies the two-question test or classifies by size, and requires the agent to include a case where summarizing genuinely is correct so the reader cannot pass by always answering 'clear it'; Lesson 6 (pressure_scenario) stress-tests budget triggers by introducing complications that make a trigger silently not fire, which is the failure the worked example ran into. Lessons 1, 3 and 4 carry no action card: their work lands in the exercises, which point at the reader's own session, and adding one would have made a button wall. No agentmentor-live block is used — this is a terminal and file-editing topic with no front-end rendered effect, which is the documented bad smell for that block type.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Targets an experienced agent operator, not a beginner: someone who already delegates real multi-step work and reads what comes back, whose runs fall apart only past a certain length. Hidden prerequisites removed: no model internals are required (the attention budget is introduced as a vendor's framing plus measurements, never as an account of attention mechanisms); no harness knowledge is required (every lever is available to someone who can only operate a tool, not modify it); no programming beyond reading a file; no API access, since every API-level mechanism is presented as evidence for how compaction behaves rather than as something to call; and no specific vendor, since each product surface is dated and each exercise asks the reader to find their own tool's equivalent from current documentation. The first independent action — inventorying what occupies the window before typing anything — needs only a breakdown their tool already provides, with an explicit fallback of estimating from file lengths on disk if it provides none, so it touches nothing on the unknown-concepts list. The concept load runs at five to seven new concepts per lesson, which is appropriate for this reader and deliberately above the three-to-four band reserved for on-ramp courses.
promotionNotes: Before promotion to examples/, re-open the Claude Code context-window page and the Anthropic compaction and context-editing pages and refresh anything that has moved — the survival-table caps, the beta header, the minimum trigger, and the strategy identifiers are the four most likely to have changed.
The slug is final and carries no temporary marker; the family logo is at the family root and the en locale is the source locale.

Lesson 5's boundary against the planned orchestrating-agents course should be confirmed with that course's author before both are published, so the two do not disagree about where delegation stops being a context technique.
Consider adding a second worked delegation message in Lesson 5 if reader feedback shows the single instance is not enough to generalise from.
